newsitem.title: USA: Cuba denounces U.S., says Clinton sells EU short.
newsitem.headline: Cuba denounces U.S., says Clinton sells EU short.

text.p: Cuba mounted a diplomatic offensive on Friday against what it sees as U.S. moves to toughen restrictions on business with the communist-ruled island.

Parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon denounced attempts in the U.S. Congress to harden up the Helms-Burton law against Cuba, saying the Clinton administration was not fulfilling an agreement with the European Union to ease part of the law. He told a news conference Havana would raise the matter at the United Nations.
Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina addressed the foreign diplomatic corps on the issue on Thursday afternoon and was holding separate meetings with each EU ambassador on Friday.

But a U.S. government official said the moves, Cuba-related amendments contained in a wider bill on foreign relations currently passing through Congress, were nothing "dramatic" and would not endanger April's U.S.-EU understanding on Helms-Burton.
"The Cubans have thrown out a few red herrings," said the official, speaking on condition he not be named.

By mounting an energetic diplomatic offensive, President Fidel Castro's government sought to draw the EU's attention to what it sees as a lack of commitment by President Bill Clinton to fulfilling the understanding with the EU.

"What we are now considering are new steps in Washington that are specially directed against other countries and against the alleged understanding between the United States and the European Union," Alarcon said, adding that the congressional moves had so far been kept secret.
The U.S. State Department said in written remarks after Alarcon's news conference that the relevant documents had been publicly available for weeks or months.

Cuba's indignation was based on 10 Cuba-related amendments to a bill on foreign relations approved on May 6 by the House of Representatives International Relations Committee. The amendments seek to add to the Helms-Burton law or to modify earlier legislation concerning Cuba.

However, the U.S. government official said the amendments did not amount to much and mostly related to issues such as tightening up reporting requirements on Helms-Burton. These include a provision for quarterly reports to Congress on sanctions imposed under Helms-Burton.
The U.S. official noted the bill, for the reorganization of foreign affairs agencies, was still in the early stages of progress through Congress.

Alarcon said the Clinton administration was doing nothing to stop the passage of amendments that contradicted the spirit of the agreement with the EU. He added he had the impression that to date the administration "has done absolutely nothing (to fulfil the understanding)."

Under the agreement, Europe agreed to suspend a World Trade Organisation (WTO) challenge to Helms-Burton. In return, Washington agreed to seek to change a key Helms-Burton provision barring from the United States executives of foreign companies deemed to be doing business on property expropriated from U.S. citizens or firms after Castro's 1959 revolution.
This would involve the White House seeking to obtain the power of a waiver for Title Four of Helms-Burton.

Cuba also objected to two draft bills prepared by the House panel that seek to strip or curtail use of a waiver Clinton has already used twice for Title Three of Helms-Burton, under which foreign firms may be sued for damages over expropriated property in U.S. courts.
The U.S. government official said a bill referring to Title Three had not yet been introduced in Congress and if it were, the administration had a "realistic chance" of defeating it.
He also said that while protesting over the issue at the news conference and to foreign diplomats, Cuban officials had not raised the issue at all, in Washington or Havana, with U.S. officials.

The agreement between the EU and Washington helped resolve trans-Atlantic tensions over Helms-Burton, which was rapidly approved by Clinton in March 1996 following the downing by Cuba of two small private U.S. planes off the island.
The law, adding to a 35-year U.S. embargo on Havana, drew international criticism over its provisions affecting third country firms doing business in Cuba.
